 Alleged Wheeling bank robber’s extradition on hold yet again
 By Gage Vota 
 November 21, 2026 
 4 min read 
 T-L Photo/GAGE VOTA
19-year-old Jemel Ishmael Ezekiel Smith of Martins Ferry appears in Belmont County Common Pleas court for his extradition hearing after being charged for allegedly robbing the downtown Wheeling WesBanco bank. 
 Trending
 ST. CLAIRSVILLE - The extradition of the Martins Ferry man accused of robbing the downtown Wheeling WesBanco bank is still in limbo despite two scheduled extradition hearings. 
 On Friday morning, 19-year-old Jemel Ishmael Ezekiel Smith appeared in person in Belmont County Common Pleas court following his uncooperative Zoom appearance Thursday. 
 Smith was arrested in Bridgeport on Tuesday but is wanted by authorities in Ohio County for his felony robbery charge. 
 Judge John Vavra asked Smith’s attorney, Belmont County public defender Aaron Miller, if he had explained the process of extradition to Smith with Miller, saying Smith has been completely unreceptive. 
 "I attempted to speak with him and there was no response whatsoever. He simply stared straight ahead, and that was it," Miller said. "So as far as going into things with someone who is not communicating, there is no reason to go into that with someone who won’t talk to me."
 Miller then made a motion to request an evaluation of Smith for competence to stand trial as well as evaluate for sanity.
 Vavra responded the competence of standing trial motion does not apply in the extradition hearing, since there is no trial for the hearing. 
 Vavra then attempted to explain what Smith's options were at Friday's extradition hearing. 
 "From what I see from the paperwork that has been filed, you are wanted in Ohio County, West Virginia. The allegation is that you committed the crime of robbery as a felony. Now that’s what, 15 minutes away. You think they just come and get you, but that’s not how it works," Vavra said. "How this all works is up to you. You have two choices. You can ask for what is called a full extra edition hearing. Now that wouldn’t happen today. It would probably happen Monday, or perhaps the Monday after that, or whenever the state could be prepared. If you want that hearing, let me explain how it works. It’s got nothing to do with what you did or did not do in West Virginia. In other words, we’re not dealing here with guilt or innocence in Ohio County. The only issue in this case for me is identification. So what that means is the prosecuting attorney, [Belmont County Prosecutor] Mr.[Kevin] Flanagan or one of his assistants will have a witness testify. Probably be one person. Usually, it’s a police officer, a detective, a probation or supervision officer."
 Or, Smith could waive his extradition hearing and agree to be extradited, allowing Ohio County officers to come to Belmont County and transfer him to the Ohio County jail.
 Vavra then informed the court that he was going to take a 10 minute recess for Smith to speak with Miller about his two options. 
 Following the recess, Miller returned and informed the court the brief recess was not productive. 
 "Your Honor, I’ve tried to explain as clearly as I can what the advantage is of waiving extradition versus not waiving extradition, multiple times and he does not understand. So that’s where we are," Miller said. "In his mind, even though the court advised that this has nothing to do with being guilty or not guilty, he’s not able to make that separation. I’ve explained to him the benefits of waiver versus having a full extradition hearing. He doesn’t understand that concept, and in order for him to make a knowing, intelligent, voluntary waiver to be extradited to West Virginia, he’s not able to make that."
 Vavra then made the ruling he was going to take Miller's comments as a request for a full extradition hearing.
 The hearing was then set for Nov. 30 at 1 p.m. in Common Pleas court.
